label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**About Glenmore**

I've started this a good few times this week and deleted it each time. Úna set this blog up so we'd have one place where everyone could hear the same news at the same time, whether you're in Boston or Perth or Leeds or down the road in Galway. This time I didn't use it the way it was meant to be used, and some of you heard my news second-hand, in bits. That's my own doing. So I'm going to put it all down here once, as honestly as I can, and then nobody has to piece it together from phone calls.

I've sold the house in Glenmore.

The sale was agreed on the 3rd of November, and it closes on the 15th of January 2027. I'm putting the date in plainly so that nobody hears it from anyone else.

For anyone who married into the family or was too small to remember the details, it's the old Mulkerrin place out near Oughterard, the house Tom grew up in. His grandfather Pádraig Mulkerrin built it in 1931, and there's been a Mulkerrin in it, or going in and out of it, ever since. I know what it means to people, and I know what it meant to Tom. I'm not writing as if this was a small thing or an easy one, because it wasn't.

**Why**

I'll start with the practical side, because that's where it started for me, even if it didn't end there.

Since Tom died in March 2024 I've been driving out every second week, forty minutes each way, to air the house and check the pipes. Some of you have come with me now and again and you'll know the routine. I open the windows even in the cold, run the taps, light a fire if there's time, check for anything that's come in under the doors, look at the ceilings for new stains, lock up and drive home. At first I didn't mind it at all. I think I wanted it, if I'm honest. It gave me somewhere to go and something to do with my hands, and it was the one place I could talk to Tom out loud without feeling foolish.

The house was getting tired, though, and I was too.

In September I had Ó Flaithearta's out to do a proper survey of the roof. I'd been putting it off because I had a fair idea what they'd say. The slates are gone in a lot of places and the back chimney needs serious work, and their quote came to €38,000. That's before the damp in the back bedroom, which has been creeping up the wall for a few years now and isn't going to fix itself. On top of that, the septic tank has to be replaced before the house can be sold to anyone at all, so that cost was coming either way.

I'm a retired primary teacher. I could probably have found the money for the roof if I'd decided it mattered more than anything else, and for a while I thought it did. But even with the roof done, the house would still need me to keep going out to it, and that's the part I wasn't telling anyone.

Last February, on one of those mornings with frost on everything, I slipped on the step at the back door. I came down hard and I lay there on the flags for about twenty minutes before I could get myself up. Nothing was broken, thank God. I was bruised for weeks and very shaken. I drove home that day, and I told nobody, not one of you. I'm telling you now because it's part of the truth and I said I'd put the hard parts in.

I've been afraid out there on my own ever since. I still went every fortnight, but I'd be listening to myself on the stairs and watching every step outside, and I'd be relieved getting back into the car in a way I never used to be. There's no signal worth talking about in the back of that house. If I'd hit my head that morning, I don't like to think how long it would have been before anyone wondered where I was.

So that's the plain version. I can't keep maintaining the house, and I'm frightened to be alone in it. Nobody needs to rush in and offer to do the fortnightly drive for me. I know some of you would, and I love you for it, but most of you are thousands of miles away, and the ones who aren't have their own lives and their own work. A house can't be kept going by a rota of people who feel guilty.

**The Joyces**

The buyers are a young couple called Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, so he's not a stranger to the place, and they have two small children. They want to live in the house. It isn't going to be a holiday let, or somewhere that sits empty for eleven months of the year with a key box on the wall.

There was an offer in the summer from a Dublin crowd that was higher. I'll say that straight out because some of you will hear it anyway. I took the Joyces' offer, which was lower, and I did it on purpose. The price was fair and I'm not hard up. When I met them and watched the two children running around the haggard, I knew which one I wanted.

Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum. He said it more than once, usually when somebody was getting sentimental about a bit of old furniture. He'd say, "It's a house, not a shrine." I've thought about that a great deal over the last few months. I can't promise you he'd have agreed with every part of how I've done this, but I'm fairly sure he'd have liked the idea of small children in wellies tearing up and down that boreen again.

The Joyces have said that any of the family can come out and walk the land any time. They meant it, too, and it wasn't just politeness. Aoife said she'd like to hear the stories about the place, if anyone wants to tell them. So you're not losing the right to stand in that field or walk down to the lake. If you're home and you want to go, you can.

**What we're keeping**

I know that for some of you the first question will be what happens to everything inside, so here's that part.

The dresser is going to Úna. She's had her eye on it since she was about nine, and she's the one who's always dusted it without being asked. Pádraig's fiddle is staying in the family. It isn't going anywhere near a sale, and once we've worked out who'll actually play it and not just hang it on a wall, we can talk about where it lives. All the photographs are being kept, every box and every loose one in the drawers. I'm going to try to get them sorted and scanned so that the cousins abroad can have copies, and I'll be asking for help with that, so you've been warned.

The Sacred Heart lamp is coming with me. I've never once seen that lamp out in my whole married life and I'm not going to be the one who lets it go out now. The gate sign is coming too. When I took it down to look at the screws, my eyes filled up and I had to sit in the car for a bit, so I'd say that one matters more than I'd let on.

If there's something particular you want, a cup or a picture or anything at all, tell me now, before the clearing. I'd far rather hear "I always loved the clock in the back kitchen" than have someone discover in March that it went to the charity shop.

**The memories**

I don't want this to be only roofs and septic tanks, because that's not what the house is to any of us.

Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind that house in 1979. It was raining, of course it was, and the cattle were watching over the wall as if they'd been told to. He'd planned something nicer, I think, but the weather wasn't on his side and he got impatient, so he just asked me there and then in the wet. I said yes and we went in soaking to tell his mother, and she pretended to be surprised.

All the children learned to swim in the lake below the house. You'll all remember the cold of it, that cold that gets into your bones even in August. Declan, you'll remember this better than anyone. You would not come out. I'd be standing on the shore calling you, your father would be calling you, and you'd stay in until your lips were blue and you were shaking, and then you'd tell us you weren't cold at all. I don't think I ever won that argument once.

There are hundreds more, and many of them are yours rather than mine. The Christmases, the wakes, the summers, the nights sitting up late with the fiddle out. Somebody always knocked something over. Somebody was always lost in the bog. None of that is being sold. It isn't in the deeds.

**How you found out**

This is the part I've found hardest to write.

I should have told everyone before the sale was agreed, or at the very latest the same day. I didn't. I kept meaning to sit down and do it properly, here or on the phone, and I kept putting it off. Partly I was tired. Partly, I think, I was afraid of exactly the reaction I got. By leaving it, I made sure the news went round the wrong way, through cousins and WhatsApp groups and "did you hear," which is the very thing this blog was set up to prevent.

I'm sorry for that, truly. You all deserved to hear it from me, and some of you didn't, and I'm sorry.

I'm not apologising for the decision itself. I've thought about it for the best part of two years and I believe it's the right one. But how you found out was my fault, and I own that.

Declan, you heard it from Gráinne in a WhatsApp message, not from me. That should never have happened. I know you rang me at two in the morning your time, and I know what that means. You weren't calling at that hour because you'd thought it over calmly. You were hurt. You said I was "selling Dad." I've heard that sentence in my head a lot since. And I said things back to you that I shouldn't have said. I was tired and defensive, I was half-ashamed of how you'd found out, and I took that out on you. I'm sorry for that as well.

I do regret not talking to you first. You're Tom's son and that's your grandfather's house, and you had every right to hear it from your mother and to have your say before anything was signed. I didn't give you that, and I wish I had.

I want to be honest with you, though. If you had asked me to wait until your visit next summer, I wouldn't have waited. I can't do another winter of that drive and those steps and that fear. I'd rather say that to you plainly than let you think that if I'd only asked, things could have gone differently. They'd have gone the same way. You'd just have known sooner, and you'd have heard it from me, and that's what I'm sorry about.

I'm not angry with you, Declan, not even a little. I understand why you said what you said. I think part of me has been saying it to myself every second Tuesday on that road for two years. The door is open. Ring me whenever you like, at whatever hour, and we'll talk properly, or not talk if you don't want to. I'll still be your mother either way.

**Keeping Tom**

I want to say a bit more about what you said, Declan, because I think some of the others feel it too even if they wouldn't put it that way.

For a long time after your father died, I felt the same as you do. I thought the house was him, or near enough. When I was out there, I'd hear him in the creak on the landing and see him in the chair by the range, and going out there felt like visiting him. Selling it would have felt like leaving him on his own.

What I've come round to, slowly, over the best part of two years, is that I can keep Tom's memory without keeping the house. I didn't decide that one afternoon. It took a lot of those drives. Somewhere in there I noticed I wasn't really going out to see Tom any more. I was going to check pipes and look for damp and be careful on the step. The house was turning into a job, and a frightening one, and it was taking the place of him instead of holding on to him.

Tom isn't in the slates or the chimney or the septic tank. He's in you and your sisters and your children, and in the stories, and in the way half of you can't stand at a lake without being dared to get in. He's in the fiddle and the photographs and the lamp. He's in the haggard, too, and I'll be able to walk in it whenever I like, because the Joyces have said so.

I really believe he'd rather have that house full of noise and small children than kept perfectly for his sake with nobody living in it. He said so often enough.

**Sunday the 13th of December**

Now the invitation, and I want as many of you there as can make it.

On Sunday the 13th of December we're going to have a family day out at the house, before it's cleared. Anyone who can come, come. I know that for the ones abroad it's not likely, and nobody is to feel bad about that. If you can't be there, I'll make sure there are photographs and I'll put them up here. If you want, ring in on someone's phone and we'll walk you round the rooms.

There'll be soup and sandwiches and tea, and something stronger for those who want it. Bring wellies. I mean it. The haggard will be a bog in December and the path down to the lake is worse. Bring the children if you have them. I'd love to have the house noisy one more time while it's still ours.

It isn't a wake and I don't want anyone treating it like one. Come and walk round, take a last look in every room, go down to the lake, tell the old stories and argue about whose version is right. If there's anything you want from the house, that's the day to say so, though it would be a help to me if you told me beforehand.

Declan, you're welcome too, of course you are. I know Christmas travel is dear and I know it might not be possible, and I'm not asking it as a test. If you can't come, I'll think of you on the shore, refusing to come out of the water.

**That's all of it**

I think that's everything. It's longer than I meant it to be, but I promised myself I'd say it all once and properly, and I have.

To sum it up for anyone who skipped to the end, and I know some of you do: the house is sold to a young family who are going to live in it. It closes on the 15th of January. The dresser, the fiddle, the photographs, the lamp and the gate sign are all staying with us, and the family can walk the land whenever they want. I'm sorry for how many of you found out, but not for the decision. And I'll see whoever can make it on Sunday the 13th of December, with soup on and your wellies on.

I've no doubt some of you will have more to say, and that's all right. Ring me or write to me or say it in the comments here if you'd prefer. I'd rather hear it straight from you than have it go round in bits, same as I'd rather you heard this straight from me.

Love to every one of you, near and far.
